body: {"total":6,"records":[{"title":"Completion of routine delirium screening on acute geriatric wards: a prospective observational study of 9,800 patient-shifts","authors":"Moyo-Hartley P, Dahl-Onwuachi R, Quintero-Walsh E","year":2021,"venue":"Journal of Geriatric Nursing Practice","doi":"10.5555/jgnp.2021.0319","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Background: delirium screening is widely required but rarely measured as it happens. Methods: on four acute geriatric wards, research nurses reconciled nursing records with ward lists for every patient-shift over 10 weeks. Results: of 9,800 eligible patient-shifts, 58 percent had a completed screen. Completion was 71 percent on day shifts, 62 percent on evening shifts and 39 percent on night shifts, and it was 11 percentage points lower at weekends. Screens were completed within 12 hours of ward arrival for 64 percent of admissions. Conclusions: screening failed mainly at night and at weekends, and efforts to improve it should start from the points where the process fails."},{"title":"Documented versus observed delirium screening: agreement between the nursing record and direct observation","authors":"Sandoval-Keane T, Obi-Marchetti L","year":2018,"venue":"Older Person Care Research","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We compared the nursing record with direct observation for 640 shifts on two geriatric wards. An observer shadowed the nurse responsible for each sampled patient and recorded whether the screening questions were asked. Screens documented in the record were observed in 83 percent of cases; in 17 percent a screen was documented but the questions were not asked, most often on night shifts and for patients who were asleep. Agreement was lowest for patients with severe hearing loss. The authors conclude that record review alone overestimates screening and recommend adding a sample of direct observation."},{"title":"Electronic prompts and delirium screening completion in older inpatients: an interrupted time series","authors":"Varga-Osei N, Lindqvist-Amadi J, Rourke-Tanaka S","year":2023,"venue":"Clinical Gerontology Services","doi":"10.5555/cgs.2023.0044","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We added a shift-start electronic prompt for delirium screening on three medical wards for older people and analysed weekly completion for 26 weeks before and 26 weeks after. Completion rose from 52 to 74 percent, with an immediate level change and no further trend. The increase was smallest on night shifts, from 31 to 45 percent. Time from a positive screen to medical review did not change. A concurrent staffing increase on one ward limits attribution, and nurses reported that the prompt often appeared while patients were asleep and was dismissed."},{"title":"Missed delirium screening in patients with dementia or sensory impairment on geriatric wards","authors":"Achebe-Lindgren O, Fontaine-Mbatha K","year":2020,"venue":"Older Person Care Research","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Using ward lists and nursing records for 1,450 admissions to three geriatric wards, we compared the proportion of patient-shifts with a completed delirium screen by dementia diagnosis and sensory impairment. Patients with a recorded dementia diagnosis had screens on 41 percent of shifts, compared with 66 percent for patients without dementia. Patients with severe hearing or vision loss had screens on 48 percent of shifts. Nurses' notes most often gave known confusion as the reason for not screening. Because delirium is more common in people with dementia, the groups least often screened are those at highest risk."},{"title":"Nurse-reported barriers to delirium screening: time, perceived futility and uncertainty with dementia","authors":"Harrow-Nkemelu B, Ostrowski-Fadipe A, Liang-Carvalho M","year":2016,"venue":"Nursing Education Letters","doi":"10.5555/nel.2016.0102","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We asked 214 nurses on geriatric and general medical wards to rate barriers to routine delirium screening. The barriers rated most important were lack of time at the start of a shift (68 percent), the belief that screening changes nothing if doctors do not act (54 percent), uncertainty about screening patients with dementia (49 percent) and reluctance to wake sleeping patients at night (47 percent). Nurses who had received bedside training in the screen reported fewer barriers. The findings suggest that screening completion depends on what happens after a positive screen as well as on nurse workload."},{"title":"Positive delirium screens and time to medical review on geriatric wards","authors":"Kimura-Obasi D, Wetherell-Diallo C","year":2025,"venue":"Journal of Geriatric Nursing Practice","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We followed 386 positive delirium screens on two geriatric wards to the first documented medical review of the patient's mental state. Thirty-eight percent were reviewed within 24 hours, 29 percent between 24 and 72 hours, and 33 percent had no documented review before discharge or a later negative screen. Positive screens at night or at weekends waited longest. Review within 24 hours was more likely when the nurse escalated the result by phone rather than only recording it. The authors suggest measuring the step from screen to action alongside screening completion."}]}
